migrationNotes: Spine: a coach's question of how much training is right for a beginner and for a champion is carried from Aristotle's food example to courage, anger and generosity, showing at each stop that the right amount depends on the person and is built by habit.

lesson.title: Character and the mean

lead.text: The coach's problem has a familiar kind of solution. Pick an amount that is too much and an amount that is too little. Then take the number halfway between them. That number is the arithmetic mean of the two. You find it by adding them and halving the result, and people often call it the midpoint. If 20 laps is too few for a runner and 40 is too many, the arithmetic mean is 30.

Aristotle used a different example, food for an athlete in training. He says that if ten minae of food is too much for a particular person and two minae too little, the trainer will not necessarily order the amount halfway between. A mina is a Greek unit of weight, a little under half a kilogram. Taking the midpoint would be a tidy rule, and it would give the same amount to everyone. The question is whether it works, and the first step is to find the number it produces.
Use the midpoint rule on Aristotle's numbers: ten minae of food is too much, and two minae is too little.

reveal.text: That is the arithmetic midpoint of the two amounts. Whether it is the right amount for a particular person is what Aristotle goes on to ask.

steps.headline: The midpoint is not the answer

lead.text: Aristotle's next remark is the one that matters. A trainer, he says, will not simply order the midpoint for everybody. Milo of Croton, a famous wrestler, was said to eat enormous meals, and the midpoint would be too little for a man of his size and training. For someone who has just started training, the same amount would be too much.

So the right amount does not sit at one fixed place on the scale. Each person has a range of amounts that suit them. For a champion the range lies above the midpoint, and for a beginner it lies below it. Aristotle called the right amount the mean relative to us, meaning that it depends on who we are and what we face, and cannot be read off the scale alone.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the scale from two to ten minae with each person's range marked. The arithmetic mean is the same for both, and the two ranges sit in different places. Good judgement follows the person, and a sum cannot do that.

lead.text: Aristotle applied the same thinking to character. A virtue is a lasting good trait of character, and each one concerns a particular area of feeling or action, which he called its sphere. Courage concerns fear and confidence. Too little confidence is the fault of cowardice, and too much is rashness. Courage lies between them.

The faults are called vices. The one with too little is a vice of deficiency and the one with too much is a vice of excess. The virtue is the mean between them: feeling the right amount, at the right time, towards the right things.

afterFigure.text: As with food, the right amount is relative to the person. The picture shows courage for a trained firefighter and for an untrained passer-by. Each is brave when acting within their own range. The firefighter's range sits higher on the scale, because training lets the firefighter rightly face more than an untrained person can.

steps.headline: Place courage for a trained firefighter and for an untrained passer-by.

workedSteps.text: Sphere: fear and confidence. Cowardice has too little confidence and rashness has too much.
The firefighter's right band sits higher on the scale than the passer-by's.
So courage is a mean relative to us, not one fixed point on the scale.

lead.text: The pattern repeats across the virtues. Take anger. Someone who is never angry, even when a friend is mistreated, has a fault of deficiency that Aristotle called lack of spirit. Someone who flares up at every small slight has the fault of excess, irascibility. The virtue between them is good temper: being angry at the right things, with the right people, to the right degree.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows the same sphere in two situations. A stranger who jostles you in a queue calls for very little anger. A parent whose child is in danger can rightly feel a great deal more. The virtue and the scale are the same, and the ranges differ.

Finding the two faults is a useful way to locate a virtue. Name the sphere, ask what going too far looks like and what falling short looks like, and the virtue is what remains between them. The next screen asks you to try this on generosity.

steps.headline: Place generosity between its two vices.

workedSteps.text: Name the vice of deficiency, giving too little.

lead.text: If the mean differs from person to person, how does anyone come to have a virtue? Aristotle separated two kinds of excellence. Virtues of thought, such as understanding, come mostly from teaching, which takes time and experience. Virtues of character, such as courage, come from habit. He compared character to a craft: we become builders by building and lyre players by playing the lyre, and in the same way we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave ones.

That is why a passer-by's range and a firefighter's differ. Practice reshapes what each person can rightly face. A beginner who often meets small fears bravely finds the range widening, while one who always runs from fear grows more timid.

afterFigure.text: In the picture, training has moved the band along the scale. Done often enough, an act stops being an effort and becomes a settled part of who you are. Aristotle called the process of forming character by repeated action habituation.

lead.text: Think of how Aristotle says we learn to build or to play the lyre, and apply it to character.

If the mean cannot be read off a scale, something has to find it in each case. Aristotle called that capacity practical wisdom, in Greek phronesis: the ability to see what a situation calls for and to act on it. It cannot be turned into a formula. It grows with experience, as a skilled trainer's sense of how much food a particular wrestler needs grows with years of watching bodies.

The point of having practical wisdom and the virtues is a good life. Aristotle's word for it is eudaimonia, often translated as happiness or flourishing. It does not mean a passing feeling of pleasure. It means living well, which he defined as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. Virtue is part of what makes a life go well, and does not arrive as a reward afterwards.
Back at the trainer's table, one thing is left to do. The mean relative to us can be measured against the midpoint, and the next question does that.
Go back to the scale of two to ten minae and the arithmetic mean you found at the start. Measure where the beginner's range sits against it.

reveal.text: The beginner's range lies below the midpoint of the scale, so for a beginner the mean relative to us sits below the arithmetic mean.

lesson.orientation: Locate a virtue between two vices, distinguish the mean relative to us from an arithmetic midpoint, and see how virtue is acquired.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A coach sets a drill of 20 laps. For a beginner who has only just started running, that is far too much and likely to end in injury. For a champion in training it is hardly a warm-up. The same drill is both too much and too little, and nobody thinks the coach has made a mistake. The mistake would be to hand every runner the same number.

Aristotle, who taught in Athens in the fourth century BCE, thought that character works the same way. Courage and generosity are matters of degree, and each lies somewhere between a fault of too little and a fault of too much. Where it lies depends on the person and the situation. A soldier, a bystander and a parent protecting a child may each need a different amount of nerve.

In this lesson you start with a simple way of finding the middle, see why Aristotle rejected it, and follow his account from food to courage to generosity. You finish with how people come to have these traits at all, and what the traits are for.

intro.promise: By the end you'll place a virtue between its two faults and tell Aristotle's mean from a simple midpoint.

recap.keyIdea: A virtue is a mean between two vices, and the mean is relative to us. It is not the arithmetic midpoint, and it is acquired by habit.

blocks.text: You found the midpoint of Aristotle's scale and saw why it fails for Milo and for a beginner. You placed generosity between its vices and measured a beginner's range against the midpoint.

recap.nextHook: Courage and generosity are traits of one person. The next lesson asks about a whole society, and begins with why anyone should obey a government at all.

questions.prompt: Aristotle supposes that ten minae of food is too much and two minae too little. What amount, in minae, is the arithmetic mean of the two?
hints: The arithmetic mean lies halfway between the two amounts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (2 + 10) / 2 = 6 minae. Aristotle's point is that the mean relative to us need not be this amount.

questions.onCorrect: Six minae: halfway between two and ten. Aristotle's mean relative to us need not be that amount.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the two amounts. The mean lies halfway, so halve it.
That is the gap between the two amounts. The midpoint lies halfway between them.

questions.prompt: Generosity concerns giving money. Its vice of excess is prodigality. Name its vice of deficiency.
hints: The deficient person gives too little and takes too much.
Think of the everyday word for someone who will not spend.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Meanness, also translated stinginess or illiberality.

questions.onCorrect: Meanness, also translated stinginess or illiberality: giving too little.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the excess, or belongs to another virtue. Name the fault of giving too little.

questions.prompt: According to Aristotle, do we acquire virtues of character mainly by teaching or by habit?
hints: Aristotle compares virtue with learning to build or to play the lyre.
Teaching produces virtues of thought; something else produces virtues of character.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: By habit: we become brave by doing brave acts.

questions.onCorrect: By habit: we become brave by doing brave acts.

misconceptions.feedback: Teaching mainly produces virtues of thought. Think of how you learn to build.

questions.prompt: On a scale from 2 to 10 minae of food, a beginner's right amount runs from 3 to 5 minae. How many minae below the arithmetic mean of the scale is the top of the beginner's range?
hints: Find the midpoint of the whole scale first.
The top of the beginner's range is its larger number.
Subtract the top of the range from the midpoint.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The arithmetic mean is (2 + 10) / 2 = 6 minae. The top of the beginner's range is 5, which is 6 − 5 = 1 mina below it.

questions.onCorrect: One mina below: the midpoint of the scale is 6 and the top of the beginner's range is 5.

misconceptions.feedback: Find the midpoint of the scale first. Then subtract the top of the range from it.
The range's top lies below the midpoint, so take it away from the midpoint, not the other way round.

questions.prompt: Ten minae is too much and two too little. For Milo, a champion wrestler, Aristotle says six minae would be:
hints: Milo is a champion athlete with a large body to feed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Too little. Aristotle says six would be too little for Milo and too much for a beginner.

questions.onCorrect: Too little for Milo, who is a champion with a large body to feed.

misconceptions.feedback: Six is only the arithmetic midpoint. Milo needs more than that.
Milo is a champion with a large body to feed. Ask whether six would be generous for him.

questions.prompt: What Greek word, often translated 'happiness' or 'flourishing', names the highest human good for Aristotle?
hints: It begins with the Greek prefix for 'good'.
Its second part is daimon, a guiding spirit.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Eudaimonia: living well and doing well, an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.

questions.onCorrect: Eudaimonia: living well, an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.

misconceptions.feedback: That is another Greek term. The one wanted names the highest good, often translated flourishing.

questions.prompt: Is there one right number of laps for everyone? Answer yes or no.
hints: Think of a beginner and a champion doing the same drill.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The right amount depends on the person.

questions.onCorrect: The right amount depends on the person. That is the thought behind a mean relative to us.

misconceptions.feedback: Think of a beginner and a champion doing the same drill. Would the same number suit both?

questions.prompt: Courage lies between which two vices?
questions.onCorrect: Too little confidence is cowardice and too much is rashness. Courage lies between.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are feelings, not vices of deficiency and excess. Courage concerns fear and confidence.
Those are traits of the body. The vices of courage are about fear and confidence.

questions.prompt: Why do the firefighter's and the passer-by's bands differ?
hints: Both bands are for the same virtue on the same scale.

acceptedIdeas: The right amount depends on the person and the situation.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The right amount depends on the person and the situation.

choices.label: The right amount depends on the person and the situation.

questions.onCorrect: Training changes what each person can rightly face. The mean is relative to us.

misconceptions.feedback: Firefighters feel fear too. The difference lies in what each can rightly face.
The scale is the same for both. The bands differ because the people do.

questions.prompt: On a scale from 4 to 12 units of food, a champion's right range runs from 10 to 11 units. How many units above the arithmetic mean of the scale is the bottom of that range?
hints: Find the midpoint of the whole scale first.
The bottom of the champion's range is its smaller number.
Subtract the midpoint from the bottom of the range.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The arithmetic mean is (4 + 12) ÷ 2 = 8. The bottom of the range is 10, which is 10 − 8 = 2 above it.

questions.onCorrect: Two above. The champion's mean sits above the midpoint, as the beginner's sits below it.

misconceptions.feedback: Find the midpoint of the whole scale first, then compare it with the bottom of the range.
That is the midpoint of the scale. The question asks how far the bottom of the range is above it.
